pos: n. (Johann Maier von Eck, 1486–1543, professor at Ingolstadt and Luther's most formidable Roman antagonist, who forced the issue of papal authority at the Leipzig Disputation of 1519)
etymology: German Eck, a corner, from his birthplace Egg an der Günz; his family name was Maier.
biblical_def: Johann Eck was a brilliant and combative theologian who understood Luther's position earlier and better than most of its defenders. At Leipzig in 1519 he set out to prove that the Wittenberg case entailed consequences Luther had not yet admitted, and he succeeded: pressed on the authority of the pope, Luther conceded that the papacy is of human institution, that councils may err, and that Jan Hus had been condemned for holding articles that are plainly scriptural. Eck had drawn the real line into the open, and both sides afterwards knew what the quarrel was about. He went to Rome, helped procure the bull Exsurge Domine, published it in Germany, and spent the next twenty years in controversy, drafting the Confutatio against the Augsburg Confession in 1530. Pro 18:17 is the honest comment on a disputation — “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” — and Eck was a searching neighbour. But Gal 1:8 is the standard he failed: a gospel other than the apostolic one is accursed “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach” it, and no see's authority alters that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest in words; controversy; an exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other.
webster_full: DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.
2. A contest in words; controversy.
3. An exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other, on some question proposed.
scriptures: Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.
corruption_summary: Eck did the Reformation an unintended service by forcing it to say out loud that the papacy is of human institution.
corruption_paragraphs: Luther went to Leipzig still hoping the quarrel could be settled within the existing authority, and Eck would not let him. By pressing the logic — if indulgences are indefensible, who defended them? and if a council erred at Constance, what is a council? — he compelled a clarity that the Wittenberg party had been avoiding. Rome gained a polemicist and lost the possibility of a quiet settlement. 1Pe 2:6 names the only foundation on offer: “Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious,” and the stone is Christ, not a succession.

Eck's own error is the one his whole career defends: that the authority of the church guarantees the doctrine, so that what Rome teaches must be what Scripture means. Act 4:12 will not bear it — “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” — and a system that adds merit, treasury and indulgence to that name has added another way. The recovery is to welcome a sharp opponent, since a searching neighbour exposes what a man really holds, and then to answer him from the text rather than from an office.
roots_summary: Greek onoma (G3686), a name; anathema (G331), accursed; Hebrew rib (H7379), a cause, a dispute.
roots_lines: Greek onoma (G3686) — a name, hence authority; Acts 4:12.
Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to preach good tidings; Galatians 1:8.
Hebrew rib (H7379) — a cause, a controversy; Proverbs 18:17.
Greek akrogoniaios (G204) — chief corner stone; 1 Peter 2:6.
usage: “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) — the name no office supplements.
“though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel” (Gal 1:8) — the standard above every see.
“He that is first in his own cause seemeth just” (Pro 18:17) — the use of a searching opponent.

pos: n. (Tommaso de Vio, 1469–1534, called Cajetan, Dominican cardinal and the greatest Thomist of his age, who examined Luther at Augsburg in 1518)
etymology: Latin Caietanus, of Gaeta, his birthplace; his religious name was Thomas, taken for Aquinas.
biblical_def: Thomas Cajetan was a scholar of the first rank — his commentary on the Summa is still printed with it — and as papal legate he was sent to Augsburg in 1518 to secure Luther's submission. The interviews failed because of how they were framed: Cajetan was instructed not to dispute but to require recantation, and Luther asked to be shown from Scripture where he was wrong. That exchange is the Reformation in miniature. Isa 8:20 states Luther's demand — “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” — and Act 4:19 the apostolic precedent for refusing: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.” What makes Cajetan interesting is that he was himself a careful biblical scholar who, in his late commentaries, questioned the authorship of Hebrews, doubted the canonical standing of several books Rome would soon define at Trent, and preferred the Hebrew to the Vulgate. He was answering Luther with an authority he was privately subjecting to evidence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract; to contradict a former declaration; and to prove as to try; to ascertain some unknown quality by experiment.
webster_full: RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.
2. To evince, establish or ascertain as truth, reality or fact, by argument, testimony or other evidence.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Gal 2:6
But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:
corruption_summary: Cajetan was told to demand a recantation rather than win an argument, and the instruction is the admission that the argument could not be won.
corruption_paragraphs: A church confident of its exegesis does not forbid its legate to dispute. The curial instruction at Augsburg was that Luther recant six words, not that he be refuted, and Cajetan — who could have argued with anyone in Europe — was reduced to repeating the demand. 1Th 5:21 is the method Scripture commands of the hearer: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good,” which presupposes that doctrine may be examined. Where examination is forbidden, authority has replaced truth as the ground of assent, and that substitution is the formal corruption the Reformation existed to undo.

Cajetan's private scholarship sharpens the point rather than softening it. He applied real critical judgment to the canon and the text, and would have been censured for it a generation later; Trent defined what he had left open. The recovery is the principle he was sent to deny and himself half practised: Isa 8:20 makes Scripture the standard by which every teacher, legate and council is measured, and Gal 2:6 says of the most eminent that “God accepteth no man's person.”
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451), law; teudah (H8584), testimony; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove, to test.
roots_lines: Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; Isaiah 8:20.
Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation; Isaiah 8:20.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold fast; 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek prosopon (G4383) — a face, a person; Galatians 2:6.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — Luther's demand at Augsburg.
“Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19) — the apostolic precedent.
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — the method a recantation forbids.

pos: n. (Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio, c. 1456–1527, Dominican Master of the Sacred Palace, who wrote the first official Roman reply to the Ninety-Five Theses)
etymology: Latin Prierias, of Prierio in Piedmont; Sylvester, of the woods.
biblical_def: Sylvester Prierias held the office of Master of the Sacred Palace, the papal theologian, and in 1518 produced the Dialogus against Luther — Rome's first formal answer, written, he boasted, in three days. Its argument is not exegetical but jurisdictional, and it is valuable for its candour. The universal church, he wrote, is virtually the Roman church; the Roman church is virtually the pope; therefore whoever does not rest on the teaching of the Roman church and the Roman pontiff as the infallible rule of faith is a heretic. He did not attempt to show from Scripture that indulgences are lawful; he asserted that the question was settled by who had spoken. Luther said the Dialogus taught him more than its author intended. Mar 7:9 is the Lord's own judgment on that order of authority — “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” — and Mat 15:9 its result, “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” Isa 29:13 describes a fear of God “taught by the precept of men.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tradition as the delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; and infallible as not capable of error.
webster_full: TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; the transmission of any opinions or practice from forefathers to descendants by oral communication.
2. That which is handed down from age to age by oral communication.
INFAL'LIBLE, a. Not fallible; not capable of erring; entirely exempt from liability to mistake.
scriptures: Mar 7:9
And he said unto them, Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
Col 2:22
Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men?
corruption_summary: Prierias stated the papal claim more plainly than any apologist since, and the plainness is the refutation.
corruption_paragraphs: The Dialogus is the formal principle of Rome without embarrassment: the church is the pope, and the pope is the rule of faith. Later Roman writing has softened the formula and surrounded it with qualifications, but Prierias had no reason to be careful in 1518, and what he wrote is the premise on which the indulgence traffic, the treasury of merits and the whole apparatus rested. Once stated, it can be tested, and Mar 7:9 tests it: a tradition that overrides the commandment of God is not a development of it. Col 2:22 dismisses “the commandments and doctrines of men” as things “to perish with the using.”

The formal principle of the Reformation is the direct contrary, and it is not a Protestant invention but the Lord's own practice: He answered the Sadducees from Moses, the lawyers from the law, and the devil from Deuteronomy. Isa 29:13 warns what happens to worship when the fear of God is “taught by the precept of men” — it becomes lip-service with the heart removed. The recovery is Scripture as the only infallible rule, with tradition honoured as a witness and never seated as a judge.
roots_summary: Greek paradosis (G3862), a tradition, that which is handed over; entalma (G1778), a commandment of men; mataios (G3152), vain.
roots_lines: Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition, that which is delivered; Mark 7:9.
Greek atheteo (G114) — to set aside, to reject; Mark 7:9.
Greek entalma (G1778) — an injunction, a commandment of men; Matthew 15:9.
Greek mataios (G3152) — vain, empty; Matthew 15:9.
Hebrew mitsvah (H4687) — a commandment, a precept; Isaiah 29:13.
usage: “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9) — the order he defended.
“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — the Dialogus in a clause.
“their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men” (Isa 29:13) — the worship it produces.

pos: n. (Hieronymus Emser, 1478–1527, secretary to Duke George of Saxony and a persistent opponent of Luther, who produced a rival German New Testament largely copied from the one he had condemned)
etymology: German Emser, from Ems; Hieronymus, the Greek Hieronymos, sacred name. Not Jerome the translator, nor Jerome of Prague.
biblical_def: Jerome Emser was the ducal secretary at Dresden and Luther's nearest and noisiest antagonist; because his family crest bore a goat, Luther called him the Leipzig goat and the pamphlet war between them is among the coarsest of the age. His substantial work was against Luther's German New Testament of 1522. He published a list of what he called a thousand and more errors in it, and then in 1527 brought out a Catholic German New Testament of his own — which, as everyone could see, followed Luther's rendering closely throughout, correcting it toward the Vulgate where doctrine was at stake and keeping his prose. The episode is a backhanded tribute: the translation Rome denounced became, within five years, the basis of Rome's own. 2Co 4:2 is the standard for all such work — “nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth” — and Jer 23:30 the warning to those “that steal my words every one from his neighbour.” Php 1:18 is the better note to end on, since Christ was preached in Germany from a text Emser could not improve.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation; that which is rendered from another language; and to translate as to interpret; to render into another language.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.
2. The act of translating; translation.
TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
scriptures: But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that steal my words every one from his neighbour.
Joh 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Pro 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
corruption_summary: Emser condemned a translation and then borrowed it, which is what happens when the objection is to the translator rather than to the text.
corruption_paragraphs: The thousand errors Emser catalogued were mostly not errors. A handful were real points of rendering where Luther's German carried his theology — allein durch den Glauben at Rom 3:28 is the famous instance, where the word alone is an interpretation Luther defended on the sense — and the rest were objections to a German Bible existing at all in hands Rome did not control. That his own version then followed Luther's shows where the real dispute lay. 2Co 4:2 is the test a translator must pass, and it cuts both ways: the work must be honest, and the critic must be honest about it.

The nearer corruption is the modern tribal use of translations, in which a version is praised or damned by the party that produced it rather than examined against the originals. Joh 8:32 promises that “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free,” and the knowing requires a text in the reader's own tongue, honestly rendered. Pro 30:5 says “Every word of God is pure” — the purity is the original's, and the translator's duty is to carry it over without adding his party to it.
roots_summary: Greek doloo (G1389), to adulterate, to handle deceitfully; Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal; tsaraph (H6884), refined, pure.
roots_lines: Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, to corrupt; 2 Corinthians 4:2.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness, cunning; 2 Corinthians 4:2.
Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal; Jeremiah 23:30.
Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; John 8:32.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — refined, tried, pure; Proverbs 30:5.
usage: “nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2) — the standard for translator and critic alike.
“that steal my words every one from his neighbour” (Jer 23:30) — his rival version.
“Every word of God is pure” (Pro 30:5) — the purity the translator carries over.

pos: n. (Johannes Cochlaeus, 1479–1552, German humanist turned controversialist, whose hostile life of Luther supplied Roman polemic with its portrait of him for three centuries)
etymology: Latinized from German Dobneck, by way of cochlea, a snail or spiral, punning on his birthplace Wendelstein, winding-stone.
biblical_def: Johann Cochlaeus wrote against Luther for thirty years and against Melanchthon, Bucer and the Anabaptists besides, but his lasting work is the Commentaria de Actis et Scriptis Martini Lutheri of 1549. It is a biography written to destroy, and it succeeded further than any of his arguments: the Luther of Catholic historiography until the twentieth century — driven by envy of the Dominicans, by lust, by pride, a monk who broke his vows because he could not keep them — is substantially Cochlaeus's creation, repeated by writer after writer who never checked it. Modern Catholic scholarship has largely abandoned the portrait, and honest historians of every confession now treat the Commentaria as a source for its author rather than its subject. The commandment is not ambiguous: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16), with Pro 19:5, “A false witness shall not be unpunished,” and Pro 12:22, “Lying lips are abomination to the LORD.” Eph 4:15 sets the only lawful manner of controversy: “speaking the truth in love.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calumny as slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another.
webster_full: CAL'UMNY, n. Slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another.
SLAN'DER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another.
2. Disgrace; reproach; disreputation; ill name.
corruption_summary: A libel repeated for three hundred years does not become history, and the ninth commandment binds polemicists on both sides of the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: Cochlaeus is the standing proof that the most effective weapon in a doctrinal war is often a biography. He did not refute justification by faith; he explained Luther psychologically, and a psychological explanation makes argument unnecessary. The method is in constant use still, by every party that accounts for a doctrine it dislikes by the motives of the man who taught it. Exo 20:16 forbids it flatly, and the prohibition is not suspended because the neighbour is a heretic in one's own judgment.

The duty falls on Protestants equally, which is why this entry is written as it is. Reformation polemic produced its own share of calumny against monks, popes and Jesuits, and some of it is still repeated in Protestant books. Eph 4:15 requires that the truth be spoken and that it be spoken in love, and a controversy conducted on those terms loses nothing but its lies. Pro 12:22 ends with the alternative: “but they that deal truly are his delight.”
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Pro 19:5
A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
Eph 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
roots_summary: Hebrew ed shaqer, a false witness; toebah (H8441), an abomination; Greek aletheuo (G226), to speak truth.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; Exodus 20:16, Proverbs 19:5.
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; Proverbs 19:5.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — an abomination; Proverbs 12:22.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — faithfully, truly; Proverbs 12:22.
Greek aletheuo (G226) — to speak the truth; Ephesians 4:15.

“A false witness shall not be unpunished” (Pro 19:5) — the Commentaria weighed.
“speaking the truth in love” (Eph 4:15) — the only lawful manner of dispute.

pos: n. (Gasparo Contarini, 1483–1542, Venetian statesman and cardinal, leader of the Catholic reform party, who agreed a formula of double justification with the Protestants at Regensburg in 1541)
etymology: Italian Contarini, an ancient Venetian patrician house; Gasparo, from the traditional name of one of the magi.
biblical_def: Gasparo Contarini is the most attractive figure on the Roman side of the age. A Venetian diplomat raised to the cardinalate as a layman, he had undergone in 1511 an experience he described in terms a Protestant would recognize: that no satisfaction of his own could stand before God, and that he must rest on the righteousness of Christ. He led the commission whose Consilium de Emendanda Ecclesia of 1537 catalogued the curia's abuses so frankly that it was placed on the Index. At the Colloquy of Regensburg in 1541 he and Melanchthon and Bucer agreed on an article of justification by faith in which the believer is accepted for the imputed righteousness of Christ while an inherent righteousness follows — the formula called double justification. Rome repudiated it; so did Luther and Calvin. The texts the Reformers held against it are decisive: Rom 4:6 speaks of the man “unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,” and Php 3:9 of being found in Him “not having mine own righteousness.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imputation as the act of imputing or charging; attribution; and to impute, in theology, as to charge or attribute to one what belongs to another.
webster_full: IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; generally in an ill sense.
2. In theology, the act of attributing to one what properly belongs to another; as the imputation of Christ's righteousness to believers.
IMPU'TE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of.
scriptures: Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 10:3
For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
Gal 5:4
Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace.
corruption_summary: Double justification was an honest attempt to say both things at once, and it failed because justification will not share its ground with anything inherent.
corruption_paragraphs: The Regensburg formula tried to hold that the believer is accepted on account of Christ's imputed righteousness and also that a righteousness wrought within him belongs to his justification. The Reformers saw that the second clause destroys the first, because a ground that is partly inherent is not grace but a mixture, and the conscience can never know how much of its own is required. Rom 10:3 names the failure precisely: men “going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.” Gal 5:4 is blunter: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law.”

The modern corruption is the ecumenical revival of the same device, in documents that declare the sixteenth-century condemnations no longer to apply while leaving the Tridentine canons in force. Contarini's attempt deserves more respect than its descendants, because he genuinely believed both halves and was trying to state a conversion he had actually had. But the distinction that must be kept is the one the Reformation made and never conceded: sanctification is real, inward and necessary, and it is the fruit of justification, never a part of its ground. Rom 4:6 gives the ground, “without works.”
roots_summary: Greek logizomai (G3049), to impute, to reckon; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; hupotasso (G5293), to submit.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to impute; Romans 4:6.
Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; Romans 4:6, Philippians 3:9.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to submit, to subject oneself; Romans 10:3.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to make of no effect; Galatians 5:4.
Greek ekpipto (G1601) — to fall out of, to fall from; Galatians 5:4.
usage: “unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6) — the ground that admits no addition.
“not having mine own righteousness” (Php 3:9) — against an inherent ground.
“going about to establish their own righteousness” (Rom 10:3) — the failure named.

pos: n. (Reginald Pole, 1500–1558, English cardinal and last Roman Catholic Archbishop of Canterbury, papal legate who restored England to Rome under Mary and presided over the church during the Marian burnings)
etymology: Latin Reginaldus, from Germanic Raginwald, counsel-power; Pole, a Yorkshire family name, his mother being Margaret, Countess of Salisbury.
biblical_def: Reginald Pole was of royal blood, a cousin of Henry VIII, and broke with the king over the divorce and the supremacy; his mother and brother were executed in the aftermath. Living in Italy, he joined the spirituali around Contarini and held a doctrine of justification so near the Protestant one that he was investigated for heresy and lost the papal election of 1549 by a handful of votes. Then Mary came to the throne, and Pole came home as legate, absolved the realm, and in 1556 was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury on the day after Cranmer burned. He presided over a church that burned nearly three hundred people in four years. He argued for instruction and for restoring church property rather than for haste, and he signed no death warrants himself; he also did not stop it, and he was the spiritual head of the realm while it happened. Joh 16:2 is the Lord's own account of such a time: “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.” Rev 17:6 describes the woman “drunken with the blood of the saints.” Pole died twelve hours after Mary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed or mode of worship.
webster_full: PERSECU'TION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed or mode of worship.
2. The state of being persecuted.
M'ARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
scriptures: Joh 16:2
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Rev 17:6
And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
corruption_summary: Pole held something close to the gospel in Italy and governed the church that burned men for holding it in England, which is what happens when a doctrine is a private opinion and not a confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The hardest fact about Pole is not that he was a persecutor by temperament — he was not — but that his own convictions on justification did not restrain him. In Viterbo he had encouraged men to rest on Christ's imputed righteousness; in Canterbury he presided while Latimer, Ridley, Hooper and Cranmer died for teaching it publicly. A conviction held privately, which yields to the church's authority when the two conflict, is not a confession at all, and the Marian fires are the measure of the difference. Luk 9:55 is the Lord's word to disciples who wanted fire called down: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.”

The corruption to name plainly is the principle that the civil sword may be used against heresy, which Rome held and which some Protestant establishments afterwards held too — Geneva, Zurich and England each have blood to answer for. It is wrong in every hand that wields it. Joh 16:2 warns that the persecutor will be sincere, and sincerity is no defence. The 1689 Confession draws the line the sixteenth century could not: the magistrate has no authority over the faith and worship of the saints, and the church's weapons are not carnal.
roots_summary: Greek latreia (G2999), religious service; methuo (G3184), to be drunken; apokteino (G615), to kill.
roots_lines: Greek latreia (G2999) — divine service, worship; John 16:2.
Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill, to put to death; John 16:2, Matthew 23:37.

Greek martus (G3144) — a witness, a martyr; Revelation 17:6.
Greek lithoboleo (G3036) — to stone; Matthew 23:37.

“drunken with the blood of the saints” (Rev 17:6) — four years, three hundred dead.
“Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55) — said to disciples who wanted fire.

pos: n. (Girolamo Seripando, 1493–1563, Augustinian general and cardinal, papal legate at Trent, who argued for double justification and was defeated)
etymology: Italian Seripando, a Neapolitan family name; Girolamo, the Italian form of Jerome.
biblical_def: Girolamo Seripando was prior general of the Augustinian order and one of the most learned men at the Council of Trent, where he returned as papal legate in its final sessions. As an Augustinian he had read Augustine on grace more carefully than most of the council, and in the debates on justification in 1546 he pressed the view that the believer's inherent righteousness is never sufficient and that he is finally accepted for the imputed merit of Christ — the position the Jesuits and the majority defeated. The decree as passed made justification consist in the infusion of a righteousness by which the man is actually made just, with increase by merit, and anathematized the Protestant article. Seripando drafted much of the council's language and submitted to what he could not carry. The Scriptures he reached for are the ones the Reformation rested on: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19), and 2Co 5:21, that He was made “sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” Jer 23:6 gives the Messiah's name: “THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merit as desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward; and righteousness, in theology, as the perfect obedience of Christ imputed to believers.
webster_full: RIGHT'EOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
2. Applied to God, the perfection or holiness of his nature.
3. The active and passive obedience of Christ, by which the law of God is fulfilled.
scriptures: Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Jer 23:6
In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:
corruption_summary: Trent had the better Augustinian in the room and voted against him, which settled the question for Rome and against Augustine.
corruption_paragraphs: Seripando's defeat is the decisive moment of the council for the doctrine of salvation. He was not a Protestant and did not wish to be; he wanted the council to say that a man's own righteousness, however real, is never the ground of his acceptance. The majority said instead that justification is an infusion by which a man is made just, that it is increased by good works, and that whoever says the sinner is justified by faith alone is anathema. 2Co 5:21 is the verse the decree cannot absorb: the exchange runs both ways, our sin to Him and His righteousness to us, and an infused quality is not an exchange.

The modern corruption is the claim that Trent and the Reformation were talking past each other about words, so that the condemnations may now be regarded as spent. Seripando is the refutation: a man inside the council, in its own vocabulary, proposed the imputation the Reformers taught, and the council rejected it knowingly and anathematized it by name. 1Co 1:30 states the alternative without remainder — Christ “of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” — and righteousness there is something He is made unto us, not something infused into us by degrees.
roots_summary: Greek hupakoe (G5218), obedience; kathistemi (G2525), to constitute, to make; hamartia (G266), sin.
roots_lines: Greek hupakoe (G5218) — obedience, submission; Romans 5:19.
Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to constitute, to appoint, to make; Romans 5:19.
Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, and a sin-offering; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — righteousness; Jeremiah 23:6.
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption, a releasing; 1 Corinthians 1:30.
usage: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19) — the position he pressed.
“that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21) — the exchange the decree could not absorb.
“THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS” (Jer 23:6) — the Messiah's own name.

pos: n. (Peter Canisius, 1521–1597, Dutch Jesuit, called the second apostle of Germany, whose catechisms and colleges recovered Austria and Bavaria for Rome)
etymology: Latinized from Dutch Pieter Kanis; Canisius plays on canis, a dog — the Dominicans' old pun, here attached to a Jesuit.
biblical_def: Peter Canisius was the first Dutchman to enter the Society of Jesus and spent forty years in Germany doing what the Protestants had done and Rome had not: catechizing. His Summa Doctrinae Christianae of 1555 and the two shorter catechisms that followed were printed in some four hundred editions in his lifetime, graded for scholars, children and the simple, in question and answer. He founded colleges at Vienna, Prague, Ingolstadt, Munich and Fribourg, preached, visited, and advised princes. He is the clearest proof that the Counter-Reformation was won in schoolrooms. The principle is Scripture's own and belongs to no party: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6); “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4); and Psa 78:5, where God “established a testimony in Jacob…that they should make them known to their children.” What was taught in those books was Trent, and so the method was right and the content was the error.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
2. An elementary book containing a summary of principles in any science or art, but appropriately in religion, reduced to the form of questions and answers.
CAT'ECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Psa 78:5
For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children:
Mat 18:6
But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.
corruption_summary: Canisius beat the Protestants at catechizing, and the lesson for a Reformed church is about the method before it is about the man.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation began with catechisms — Luther's Small Catechism, the Heidelberg, the Genevan, later the Westminster Shorter and the Baptist Catechism — and wherever it stopped using them it lost ground. Canisius understood that a generation is held by whoever teaches its children, and he out-worked the Lutherans in their own territories. Pro 22:6 and Eph 6:4 are not denominational property; the household and the church that neglect them will lose their children to whoever does not. The sharpest rebuke a Reformed reader can take from this entry is that a Jesuit took the family and the schoolroom more seriously than many Protestants then or now.

The content is the other half, and it must be named. The doctrine those four hundred editions carried was Trent's: justification by infused righteousness increased by merit, seven sacraments, the invocation of saints, purgatory, the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice. Mat 18:6 is a terrible word about what is taught to little ones — “whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck.” Method without truth is efficient harm. The recovery is to catechize as diligently as Canisius did, out of a confession that is scriptural.

pos: n. (Roberto Bellarmino, 1542–1621, Italian Jesuit cardinal, author of the Disputations on the Controversies of the Christian Faith, the most formidable Roman case against Protestantism ever written)
etymology: Italian Bellarmino, from bello, fair, and arme, arms; Roberto, Germanic Hrodebert, bright in fame.
biblical_def: Robert Bellarmine held the chair of controversies at the Roman College and produced, between 1586 and 1593, the three folio volumes that organized the entire Protestant case and answered it point by point. The Disputationes are remarkable for their method: Bellarmine states his opponents' arguments fully, in their own words, with their proof texts, before replying — so fairly that English divines suspected him of helping the Protestant cause, and the work was for a time the best summary of Reformed doctrine available in Latin. Every Reformed scholastic of the next century cut his teeth on him: Whitaker, Ames, Chamier, Turretin, Owen, and Chandieu before them all. Cambridge and Oxford endowed lectures to refute him. The pattern of such labour is 2Co 10:5, “Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God,” and Pro 27:17, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.” 1Ti 1:3 states the charge he and his opponents both believed they were keeping, “that they teach no other doctrine.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controversy as a disputation, particularly in writing; a contest of opinions; and a controvertist as one who carries on a controversy.
webster_full: CON'TROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
2. A disputation, particularly in writing; a contest of opinions in speech or writing.
CONTROVERT'IST, n. One who controverts; a disputant; a man versed or engaged in controversy or disputation.
scriptures: Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine,
Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.
corruption_summary: Bellarmine is the best Rome could do, and the Reformed answer to him is the reason Reformed theology acquired its precision.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a mistake to treat Bellarmine as a hack. He knew the Fathers better than most of his opponents, argued from Scripture at length, and conceded points where the evidence ran against him — he allowed that the word of God is the rule of faith, and then located its interpretation in the church's magisterium, which is where the real argument lies. That is why answering him was so profitable: a strong opponent forces an exegete to prove what he had been assuming, and Reformed theology after 1600 is sharper, better organized and better read in the Fathers because Bellarmine existed. Pro 27:17 is literally true of this history.

His decisive error is the one he placed at the foundation: that Scripture is sufficient as a rule but insufficient as a judge, so that the church must determine its sense. Mat 22:29 is the Lord's own refutation of the move, since He charges the Sadducees with error for “not knowing the scriptures” — which assumes that the Scriptures carry a knowable sense by which even the religious authorities may be convicted. Once the magisterium is made the judge, the rule cannot correct the judge, and every later addition is secure. The recovery is Scripture interpreting Scripture, the plain sense ruling, and the church a servant of the text.
roots_summary: Greek logismos (G3053), a reasoning, an imagination; hupsoma (G5313), a high thing; planao (G4105), to err, to be led astray.

Greek aichmalotizo (G163) — to bring into captivity; 2 Corinthians 10:5.

“Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17) — literally true of the Reformed answer to him.
“Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures” (Mat 22:29) — the Scriptures carry a knowable sense.
